1.Definition of key terms
1.1. FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
FTP, or File Transfer Protocol, is a standard network protocol used for
transferring files between a client and a server over the Internet. It facilitates the
exchange of commands and data, allowing users to upload or download files to
and from a remote server. FTP operates using two modes: Active and Passive,
which determine how data connections are established. While FTP is widely used
for website management and file sharing, it does not encrypt data during
transmission, making it vulnerable to interception. To enhance security,
variations like FTPS (FTP Secure) and SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) are often
used, which encrypt the data being transferred.
Types of FTP
o FTP secure (FTPS): Taking security one notch up from traditional FTP, FTP Secure
(FTPS) ensures a secure file transfer. It provides an additional encryption layer
using either Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) or Transport Layer Security (TLS)
protocols during data transmission across the network.
o SSH file Transfer Protocol (SFTP): This is a secure file transfer subsystem for the
Secure Shell (SSH) protocol. SFTP is a widely used method for securely
transferring files over remote systems. In SFTP, both data and commands are
encrypted and transmitted in specifically formatted binary packets through a
single, secured connection using SSH.

Speed and reliability are crucial factors to consider when choosing an FTP client.
A client with fast transfer speeds will save you valuable time, especially when
dealing with large files or a high volume of data. Additionally, a reliable FTP client
will ensure that your files are transferred without any interruptions or errors,
minimizing the risk of data loss.
2. Security: Ensure that the FTP client supports secure connection protocols such as

of utmost importance when transferring files over the internet. It is essential to
choose an FTP client that supports secure connection protocols like FTPS (FTP
over SSL/TLS) or SFTP (SSH File Transfer Protocol) to encrypt your data and
protect it from potential threats.

Indicative content 6.2: Configure the FTP Server

directory with its respected features.

Key readings 6.2.1: Setup root directory for the FTP server
1.Root directory for the FTP server
To this point, we have installed the FTP server feature on the system, and a root
default directory is created to that effect. The path of the root directory is
at C:\inetpub.
We are going to create a custom FTP directory where we are going to place files
and directories which can be accessed by authorized users across the network.
Therefore, navigate to the C:\inetpub path. Right click and select ‘New’
then ‘Folder’. Give the folder your preferred name. In this case, we have created
a folder called myFTPdirectory.
2.Access permissions
Access permissions for files and directories in an FTP server can be categorized
into three main types: Read, Write, and Execute. Here’s a detailed overview of
each type of permission:
2.1. Read Permission (r): Allows users to view the contents of a file or directory.
For directories, this permission enables users to list the files contained within
that directory. Without read access, users cannot see or retrieve any files.
2.2. Write Permission (w): Grants users the ability to modify a file or directory.
Duration: 3 hrs
Practical Activity 6.2.1: Setup root directory for the FTP server
Task:

-- 244 of 319 --

234 | W i n d o w s S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
For files, this means they can edit the content or overwrite it. For directories,
write permission allows users to create new files or subdirectories and delete
existing ones.
2.3. Execute Permission (x): This permission is relevant primarily for directories
in the context of FTP servers. It allows users to enter a directory and access its
contents if they have read permission.
We need to assign this directory the required permissions so that an authorized
user can read from its contents. To achieve this, right-click on the directory and
select ‘Properties’.
In the ‘Properties’ window pop-up, click on the ‘Security’ tab to adjust the
permissions. Select the group which you want to allow access to the directory. In
this case, I have selected the ‘Users’ group. Then click on the ‘Edit’ button to
assign permissions to the group.

as needed.

3.Enable Logging (Optional)
To enable logging for an FTP server on Windows Server, you can follow these
steps to configure logging through the Internet Information Services (IIS)
Manager:
o Open IIS Manager: Go to Start > Server Manager > Tools> Internet Information
Services (IIS) Manager.
o Select Your FTP Site, In the IIS Manager, locate your FTP site under the Sites
node.
o Configure Logging, with your FTP site selected, look for the FTP Logging feature
in the middle pane. Double-click on FTP Logging to open the configuration
settings.
o Enable Logging, Check the box for Enable logging if it is not already checked.
o Choose Log File Format, you can select the log file format. The default is usually
W3C format, which is recommended for its compatibility with various log
analysis tools.
o Specify Log File Directory, you can specify a custom directory for your log files if
you wish. By default, logs are stored in: %SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs\LogFiles
o Configure Log File Settings, Set options for log file rollover and retention, such
as:
o Log file rollover: Choose how often logs should be rolled over (daily, weekly, or
monthly).
o Log file size limits: You can set limits on log file sizes to manage disk space
effectively.
o Click Apply in the Actions pane to save your logging settings.
o Restart FTP Service (if necessary):
▪ If you made significant changes to the configuration, consider restarting the FTP
service to ensure that all settings take effect:
▪ Open the Services snap-in (Start > Administrative Tools > Services).
▪ Find Microsoft FTP Service, right-click it, and select Restart.
4.Test FTP server
To test if your FTP server is working as expected head over to a remote system

# Indicative content 6.3: Implement FTP Server File Sharing

Indicative content 6.3: Implement FTP Server File Sharing

asked to go to the computer lab to perform the following: choose FTP software and set
permissions to the directory.

Key readings 6.3.1.: Choose FTP Server Software
1. Choose an FTP server software
When choosing an FTP server software, several options stand out based on
features, security, and usability. Here’s a concise overview of some of the best
FTP server solutions available:
1.1. Top FTP Server Software
o SolarWinds Serv-U Managed File Transfer (MFT): comprehensive FTP server that
offers robust encryption for secure file transfers. Supports SFTP and FTP/S for
enhanced security. User-friendly interface with management tools for tracking
file activity. Ideal for businesses needing compliance and secure file handling.
o Cerberus FTP Server: Designed for Windows, Cerberus is known for its ease of
use and strong security features. Supports multiple protocols including SFTP,
FTPS, and HTTPS. Features two-factor authentication and detailed user
management options.
o Complete FTP: A versatile FTP server suitable for larger organizations with
diverse file transfer needs. Supports various protocols (FTP, SFTP, FTPS) with
enterprise-level options like clustering. High availability and scalability to handle
extensive data transfers.
o FileZilla Server: An open-source solution that is popular for its simplicity and
ease of use. Supports FTP and FTP over TLS for secure connections. Basic
functionality suitable for internal file transfers but lacks advanced enterprise
features.
o Good Sync: While primarily a backup solution, Good Sync can function as an FTP
server with synchronization capabilities. Automated backup and synchronization
Duration: 3 hrs

Task:

-- 259 of 319 --

249 | W i n d o w s S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
across multiple devices. Highly reliable for businesses with varied data
management needs.
1.2. Considerations When Choosing an FTP Server
- Security: Ensure the server supports secure protocols like SFTP or FTPS to
protect data in transit.
-Usability: Look for user-friendly interfaces that simplify management tasks.
-Support & Documentation: Reliable customer support and comprehensive
documentation can ease the setup and maintenance process.
To implement FTP server file sharing, follow these steps, including choosing an
FTP server software, setting permissions for a shared directory, and testing the
setup.
Choose an FTP Server Software
For this implementation, we will use FileZilla Server due to its user-friendly
interface and robust features. It supports both FTP and FTPS, making it suitable
for secure file transfers.
Installation Steps:
-Download FileZilla Server: Obtain the installer from the official FileZilla website.
-Run the Installer: Follow the prompts to complete the installation.
-Launch FileZilla Server Interface: Open the application after installation.
2. Set Permissions for Shared Directory
2.1. Create a Shared Directory
✓ Create a Directory: On your server, create a directory that you want to
share (e.g., C:\FTPShared).
✓ Set Folder Permissions:
Right-click on the folder and select Properties.
Go to the Security tab and set permissions for users or groups as
needed (e.g., allowing read/write access).
2.2. Configure User Permissions in FileZilla
1. Open the FileZilla Server Interface.
2. Go to Edit > Users.
3. Click on Add to create a new user account (e.g., ftpuser).
4. Set a password for the user.
5. Under the Shared folders section:
-Click on Add to include your shared directory (C:\FTPShared).
-Set permissions:
-Read: Allows the user to view files.
-Write: Allows the user to upload files.
-Delete: Allows the user to delete files.
-Create: Allows the user to create new directories.
6. Click OK to save changes.

-- 260 of 319 --

250 | W i n d o w s S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
3. Test FTP File Sharing
Testing Steps:
1. Use an FTP client like FileZilla Client, WinSCP, or any other FTP client.
2. Connect to your FTP server using the following credentials:
-Host: Your server's IP address or hostname.
-Username: ftpuser (or whatever username you created).
-Password: The password you set for the user account.
-Port: 21 (default for FTP).
3. Once connected, navigate to the shared directory (`C:\FTPShared`).
4. Try uploading a file to ensure write permissions are correctly set.
5. Attempt to delete a file (if applicable) to confirm that delete permissions work
as intended.
4. Verification
Ensure that you can view, upload, and delete files based on the permissions set
for the user account. If any issues arise during testing, revisit the permission
settings in both Windows and FileZilla Server.

Key readings 7.1.1.: Description of load balancer installation
1. Load balancing
Load balancing is the process of distributing traffic among multiple servers to
improve a service or application's performance and reliability.
2. DNS-based load balancing
DNS-based load balancing is a specific type of load balancing that uses the DNS
to distribute traffic across several servers.
3. Hardware load balancers
These are specifically designed to provide the best load balancing based on the
task they are intended to address.
4. Software load balancers
These are the applications that can be installed and provisioned on more
traditional compute resources like servers.
5. Layer 4 load balancing
It manages traffic based on network information such as protocols and
application ports without requiring visibility into actual content of messages.
6. Layer 7 load balancing
It operates at the application layer of the OSI model, allowing for more
sophisticated traffic management compared to Layer 4 load balancing.

Key readings 7.1.2 Description of load balancing
Load balancing is the process of distributing traffic among multiple servers to
improve a service or application's performance and reliability.
This process enhances the performance, reliability, and availability of
applications and services.
Key Aspects of Load Balancing
1. Purpose:
Load balancing aims to optimize resource utilization, improve response times,
and increase the availability of applications. By evenly distributing traffic, it
prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck, which can lead to
performance degradation or downtime.
2.How It Works:
• A load balancer acts as an intermediary between clients and servers. When a
client makes a request, the load balancer determines which server is best suited
to handle that request based on various algorithms and criteria. It then forwards
the request to the selected server.
3.Types of Load Balancers:
Load balancers can be hardware-based or software-based.
• Hardware load balancers are dedicated devices that provide high performance
but can be expensive
• Software load balancers run on standard servers or virtual machines and are
more flexible and scalable.
4.Load Balancing Algorithms:
Various algorithms dictate how requests are distributed among servers:

• Round Robin: Distributes requests sequentially across servers.
• Least Connections: Directs traffic to the server with the fewest active
connections.
• Least Response Time: Chooses the server with the lowest average response
time.
• IP Hash: Uses the client's IP address to determine which server will handle the
request, ensuring session persistence.
5.Benefits:
• The primary benefits of load balancing include improved application
performance, increased reliability through redundancy, better resource
utilization, enhanced user experience due to faster response times, and
scalability to handle varying levels of traffic.
• In summary, load balancing is essential for modern applications that require high
availability and performance.

Key readings 8.1.1.: Description of Windows server update service
1.Windows server update service
This is a Microsoft tool that enables IT administrators to manage the
distribution of updates released by Microsoft to computers in a corporate
environment. It serves as a local update management system, where admins
can decide which updates are approved for installation on networked devices.
Here’s a detailed overview:
Key Features:
Centralized Management:
WSUS allows administrators to manage the deployment of updates for
Windows operating systems, Microsoft Office, and other Microsoft software
products from a central server.
Administrators can approve, schedule, and control the distribution of updates
to individual computers or groups of computers.
2.Update Categories:
• It supports updates for various categories such as critical updates, security
updates, service packs, feature packs, and drivers.
• Administrators can select which types of updates they want to deploy based on
their relevance and importance.
3.Control over Deployment:
• Administrators can test updates in a controlled environment before deploying
them network-wide, ensuring that updates do not interfere with critical
business functions.
Duration:4 hrs

• It allows granular control by offering the ability to approve or decline updates,
automatically approve certain update types, and schedule installations.
4.Network Efficiency:
• By downloading updates from Microsoft once and distributing them locally,
WSUS reduces bandwidth consumption, as each client does not need to
connect to the internet for updates.
5.Reporting:
WSUS provides detailed reports on the status of updates, helping
administrators track which updates have been installed and on which
machines.
How WSUS Works:
Synchronization with Microsoft Update:
• WSUS connects to the Microsoft Update server to download the latest updates.
• Administrators can choose to synchronize all available updates or only those
relevant to their environment.
Client-Side Interaction:
• Client computers are configured to contact the WSUS server instead of
Microsoft's online update service for updates.
• Based on the policies set by the administrator, clients download and install
approved updates.
Deployment and Monitoring:
Administrators can monitor the status of updates and generate reports to
ensure that updates are successfully installed and that no issues arise during
the process.
summary, WSUS is a powerful tool for managing updates in a Windows
environment, offering centralized control, testing, and monitoring, making it an
essential tool for IT administrators looking to maintain a secure and efficient
network.

Key readings 8.1.2: Installing the necessary roles and features
steps of Installing the necessary roles and features in windows server 2019
Here’s a step-by-step guide to installing roles and features in Windows Server
2019:
Method 1: Using Server Manager
Step 1: Open Server Manager
• Open Server Manager by clicking the Start button and selecting Server Manager
from the menu.
Step 2: Add Roles and Features
• In Server Manager, click on Manage in the upper-right corner.
• Select Add Roles and Features from the dropdown menu.
Step 3: Before You Begin
• A "Before You Begin" window will appear. Review the information and click Next.
Step 4: Installation Type
• Choose Role-based or feature-based installation, then click Next.
Step 5: Select Destination Server
• Choose the server where you want to install the roles and features. Typically, it’s
your local server. Select the server from the Server Pool and click Next.
Step 6: Select Server Roles
• In the Server Roles window, you’ll see a list of available roles. Check the box for
the roles you want to install (e.g., Active Directory Domain Services, DNS Server,
Web Server (IIS), etc.).
• After selecting a role, you may be prompted to install additional features
required for that role. Click Add Features when prompted, and then click Next.
Step 7: Select Features
• In the Features window, you can add additional features if necessary (e.g., .NET
Framework 3.5, Failover Clustering).
• Once selected, click Next.
Step 8: Role Services (Optional)
• If installing a role like Web Server (IIS), you will be asked to select Role Services.
Check any additional services you need and click Next.
Step 9: Confirm Installation Selections
• Review your selected roles, features, and services. You can also choose to restart
the server automatically if required. If you’re ready, click Install.
Step 10: Installation Progress
• The installation will begin. You can monitor the progress, and once it’s complete,
you’ll receive a confirmation message.

Key readings 8.2.1: Configuration of WSUS
1.Step Configure WSUS
• Open WSUS Console:
In Server Manager, navigate to Tools > Windows Server Update Services.
2. Run Configuration Wizard:
The WSUS Configuration Wizard should start automatically. If it doesn't, you can
manually launch it from the WSUS console under Options > WSUS Server
Configuration Wizard.
3.Choose Upstream Server:
Select whether to synchronize updates from Microsoft Update or another WSUS
server. For a new setup, choose to synchronize from Microsoft Update
4.Configure Group Policy Settings:
To direct client machines to your new WSUS server, configure Group Policy settings
that specify the WSUS server's location (e.g., http://<YourServerName>:8530). This
can be done through Group Policy Management Editor under Computer
Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > Windows Components >
Windows Update
5.Finalize Configuration:
After configuration, approve updates in the WSUS console as needed and ensure
clients are reporting correctly to your WSUS server.
• Approve Updates
After synchronization, review available updates in the WSUS console and approve

Key readings 8.3.1.: Description of server backup
1.Definition of key terms
1. A server backup is a copy of the data stored on a server. The backup should be
made to a different media and ideally stored in a different location. Backups provide
an accessible copy of the data on the server, allowing it to be recovered if the
original data is lost or corrupted.
2. A recovery strategy in computer science refers to a plan designed to restore a
database system to a working state after a failure or disaster.
Assess data to be backed up
Identify critical data, including user files, system configurations, databases, and
applications, that need to be backed up to ensure business continuity.
Plan the Backup and recovery strategies
Develop a comprehensive backup and recovery plan outlining the frequency of
backups, retention policies, and recovery procedures.
Backup type
1.full backups
A full backup is the process of creating one or more copies of all organizational data
files in a single backup operation to protect them.
incremental backups
is a backup type that only copies data that has been changed or created since the
previous backup activity was conducted.
Duration: 3 hrs

291 | W i n d o w s S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
3. differential backups
is a data protection method that copies all files changed since the last full backup.
Select Backup Location
Determine where backups will be stored, considering factors like accessibility,
security, and redundancy. For example, you may choose to store backups on local
storage devices, network-attached storage (NAS), or cloud storage services like AWS
S3 or Azure Blob Storage.
Schedule Backups
•Establish a backup schedule that ensures regular and consistent backups are
performed according to the defined backup strategy. For example, you may
schedule daily backups during non-business hours to minimize disruption.
✓ Secure Backup Storage:
•Implement security measures to protect backup data from unauthorized access,
tampering, or loss. This may include encryption, access controls, and physical
security measures for storage devices.
Test Restorations
Regularly test the restoration process to verify the integrity and effectiveness of
backups. Conducting periodic recovery drills helps ensure that data can be
successfully restored in the event of a disaster.
Documentation of backup
Maintain detailed documentation of the backup process, including backup
schedules, storage locations, and recovery procedures. This documentation serves
as a reference for IT staff and facilitates compliance with regulatory requirements.
Regularly review
Periodically review and evaluate the backup strategy to ensure it remains aligned
with changing data and server requirements. Adjustments may be necessary as new
applications are deployed or data volumes increase.
Update backup strategy as your data and server requirements evolve
Update the backup strategy as your data and server requirements evolve,
incorporating lessons learned from past backup and recovery experiences.
Periodic mock drills
Conduct periodic mock drills to simulate various disaster scenarios and test the
effectiveness of the backup and recovery procedures. This helps identify potential
weaknesses and areas for improvement.
Produce DRP document
Develop a Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP) document that outlines the steps to be
taken in the event of a server failure or data loss. This document should include
roles and responsibilities, escalation procedures, and contact information for key
stakeholders.

The migration process in Windows Server refers to the transfer of roles, features,
and data from one server to another. This process ensures minimal downtime and
data integrity. Below is a general guide to performing a migration in a Windows

Steps to Perform Migration in Windows Server

and data to be migrated.
2. Check compatibility: Ensure the destination server is compatible with the roles
and applications running on the source server.
3. Backup source server: Always back up the source server and its critical data before
performing any migration.
4. Gather necessary tools: Install the Windows Server Migration Tools and other
relevant migration software.

source server.

INTRODUCTION
This trainee's manual includes all the knowledge and skills required in Network and Internet
Technologies specifically for the module of "Linux Server Administration". Trainees enrolled
in this module will engage in practical activities designed to develop and enhance their
competencies. The development of this training manual followed the Competency-Based
Training and Assessment (CBT/A) approach, offering ample practical opportunities that mirror
real-life situations.
The trainee's manual is organized into Learning Outcomes, which is broken down into
indicative content that includes both theoretical and practical activities. It provides detailed
information on the key competencies required for each learning outcome, along with the
objectives to be achieved.
As a trainee, you will start by addressing questions related to the activities, which are
designed to foster critical thinking and guide you towards practical applications in the labor
market. The manual also provides essential information, including learning hours, required
materials, and key tasks to complete throughout the learning process.
All activities included in this training manual are designed to facilitate both individual and
group work. After completing the activities, you will conduct a formative assessment, referred
to as the end learning outcome assessment. Ensure that you thoroughly review the key
readings and the 'Points to Remember' section.

Key readings 1.1.1: Description of Linux server Operating System
1. Definition of Linux Server OS
A Linux server OS is an open-source operating system designed to manage servers,
applications, and network resources. It provides high performance, stability, and
security, which makes it a popular choice for web servers, database servers, and
other network services.
2. Key Features of Linux Server Operating Systems
• Security: Linux is known for its robust security features, including built-in
firewalls (e.g., iptables), user account management, and access controls.
• Stability and Reliability: Linux servers are highly stable and can run for long
periods without crashing or requiring reboots, making them ideal for critical
enterprise applications.
• Open source and customization: Linux is open-source, meaning administrators
can customize the system to suit their needs. There are various Linux
distributions (e.g., Ubuntu, CentOS, Red Hat) tailored to different use cases.

3. Essential components of a Linux server operating system and their roles are:
• Kernel: The core component that manages hardware resources and ensures
secure communication between hardware and software.
• Shell: Provides a command-line interface for users to interact with the system,
execute commands, and run scripts.
• File System: Manages how data is stored, accessed, and organized on storage
devices, ensuring file security and efficient access.
• Daemon: Background services (like web servers, mail servers, etc.) that run
continuously to perform tasks such as serving web pages, sending emails, or
running backups.
4. Advantages of Using a Linux Server Operating System Over Other Server
Operating Systems
• Cost Efficiency: Linux is open-source and free to use, which significantly
reduces costs for businesses compared to proprietary systems like Windows
Server.
• Security: Linux offers excellent security features with frequent updates and
community support for patches, making it harder for malware and hackers to
exploit the system.
• Customization and Flexibility: Linux provides a wide range of distributions and
configuration options, allowing users to tailor the system to meet specific
needs.
5. Common Limitations or Challenges Associated with Linux Server Operating
Systems
• Steep Learning Curve: Administrators may need specialized skills and
experience, especially for command-line management, which can be difficult
for beginners.
• Limited Support for Certain Applications: Some proprietary software and
applications may not be natively supported on Linux, requiring workarounds
like virtualization or compatibility layers (e.g., Wine).
• Hardware Compatibility: While Linux supports a broad range of hardware,
some drivers or hardware-specific features may not be as well-supported as
they are on other systems, particularly Windows.
6. Common Applications or Use Cases for Linux Servers in Enterprise Environments
• Web Hosting and Web Servers: Linux powers a majority of the world’s web
servers, often using software like Apache, Nginx, and MySQL.
• Database Servers: Many enterprises use Linux for database servers running
PostgreSQL, MySQL, or MongoDB.
• Cloud Infrastructure: Linux is widely used in cloud computing, providing the
backbone for platforms like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud, and
Microsoft Azure.

• Storage: Sufficient hard disk space for the operating system, applications, and

• Network Interface Card (NIC): At least one NIC is required for network

2. Software requirements to consider before installing a Linux server operating
system
• Supported Distribution: Choose a Linux distribution that meets your
requirements (e.g., Ubuntu Server, CentOS, Debian).
• Compatibility with Applications: Ensure that any applications you plan to run
are compatible with the chosen Linux distribution.
• Software Dependencies: Identify and install any necessary dependencies or
libraries required for your applications before installation.
• Updates and Patches: Check for the latest updates or patches for the Linux
distribution to ensure security and stability.
3. Networking requirements for setting up a Linux server
• Static IP Address: Assign a static IP address for easier access and management
of the server.
• Domain Name System (DNS): Configure DNS settings for name resolution,
allowing users to connect using domain names rather than IP addresses.
• Firewall Configuration: Set up firewall rules to allow or restrict traffic to and
from the server.
• Network Services: Depending on the server role, configure necessary
network services (e.g., DHCP, FTP, HTTP).
4. Essential security requirements for a Linux server to protect against unauthorized
access and vulnerabilities
• User Account Management: Implement strong password policies and limit
user privileges to reduce the risk of unauthorized access.
• Firewall Setup: Use tools like iptables or firewall to configure firewall rules
that restrict unauthorized access to server ports.
• Regular Updates: Keep the operating system and installed software up-to-
date with security patches and updates.
• Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS): Consider implementing
tools to monitor for suspicious activity and potential breaches.
5. Performance factors to consider when configuring a linux server
• CPU and Memory Usage: Monitor CPU and RAM usage to ensure resources
are not being over-utilized, potentially leading to slow performance.

• Disk I/O: Optimize disk read/write operations to improve data access speeds.
Consider using SSDs for faster performance.
• Network Bandwidth: Ensure sufficient network bandwidth for the server's
expected traffic load to avoid bottlenecks.
• Load Balancing: Distribute traffic across multiple servers to improve
performance and avoid overload.
6. Linux supports scalability in server environments
• Vertical Scaling: Linux can efficiently utilize hardware upgrades, such as
adding more RAM or CPUs to a single server.
• Horizontal Scaling: Multiple Linux servers can be deployed to handle
increased load, often using clustering or load-balancing techniques.
• Containerization: Technologies like Docker allow for lightweight, isolated
applications that can be easily scaled up or down.
• Considerations: Plan for resource allocation, network configurations, and
application architecture to ensure effective scaling.
7. Measures to ensure high availability and reliability of Linux servers
• Redundancy: Implement hardware and software redundancy (e.g., RAID,
clustering) to minimize downtime in case of failure.
• Load Balancing: Use load balancers to distribute incoming traffic across
multiple servers, improving performance and availability.
• Regular Backups: Schedule regular backups to prevent data loss and ensure
quick recovery in case of system failure.
• Monitoring Tools: Implement monitoring solutions to track server health
and performance, allowing for proactive management and issue resolution.

Key readings: 1.2.1: Identification of tools and equipment:
1. Server Hardware
• Processor (CPU): Choose a multi-core processor to handle multiple concurrent
tasks efficiently. Intel Xeon and AMD EPYC processors are popular choices for
server environments due to their performance and scalability.
• Memory (RAM): Aim for at least 4 GB of RAM for basic server functions, but 8
GB or more is recommended for more demanding applications, such as database
management or hosting multiple services.
• Storage:
o Type: Consider using SSDs for faster read/write speeds and better
performance, especially for applications that require quick data access.
o Capacity: Assess storage needs based on anticipated data volume; a
minimum of 100 GB is common, but this may vary based on specific
applications and data requirements.
o RAID Configuration: Implement RAID (Redundant Array of Independent
Disks) for data redundancy and improved performance. RAID 1 (mirroring)
or RAID 5 (striping with parity) are popular configurations.
• Network Interface Card (NIC): A Gigabit NIC is essential for efficient network
connectivity. Consider dual NICs for redundancy and load balancing if necessary.

needs. Apache and Nginx are popular choices, each with its strengths (Apache
for extensive features and Nginx for performance).
• Database Management System (DBMS): Select a DBMS based on the
applications you plan to run. MySQL and PostgreSQL are commonly used for web
applications and data management.
• Backup Solutions: Implement automated backup solutions such as:
o rsync: For file synchronization and backups.
o Bacula: A more comprehensive backup solution for large environments.
• Performance Monitoring Tools: Utilize tools like:
o Nagios: For system and network monitoring.
o Zabbix: For monitoring the performance of servers, applications, and
network devices.
4. Security Measures
• Firewalls: Configure a firewall (like iptables or firewalld) to control incoming and
outgoing traffic based on predetermined security rules.
• Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS): Consider using an IDS (such as Snort) to
monitor network traffic for suspicious activity.
• Regular Updates: Ensure that the Linux distribution and all installed software
receive regular updates to mitigate security vulnerabilities.
5. Documentation and Support
• Documentation: Maintain thorough documentation of the server setup,
configurations, and procedures for troubleshooting. This is essential for future
maintenance and updates.

• Community and Vendor Support: Evaluate the availability of community
support (forums, documentation) or vendor support if using a commercial
distribution. This can be crucial for resolving issues quickly.
6. Testing and Validation
• Test Environment: Consider setting up a test environment to validate the server
setup before deploying it in production. This can help identify any potential
issues with hardware compatibility or software configurations.

Selecting tools and equipment for a Linux web server
1. Server Hardware
This includes the physical equipment on which the Linux web server will run.
• CPU: Choose a server with a processor capable of handling expected web traffic
(Intel Xeon or AMD EPYC).
• RAM: Sufficient memory is necessary for smooth operation, typically starting at
8GB or more, depending on the traffic.
• Storage: provide faster read/write speeds for hosting websites and databases.
• Network Interface Card (NIC): High-speed Ethernet cards (e.g., 10Gbps) ensure
fast data transfer between server and clients.
2. Linux Distribution
The operating system that runs the server. Common Linux distributions for web
servers include:
• Ubuntu Server: User-friendly and widely supported, with a large community.
• CentOS: Known for stability, especially for enterprise applications.

• Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL): Commercial option with professional
support, ideal for critical environments.
• Debian: Known for its stability and extensive repository of software packages.
3. Web Server Software
• Apache HTTP Server: One of the most popular web server platforms, open-
source and highly configurable. And it is suitable for hosting dynamic websites
and handling large traffic.
• Nginx: A lightweight, high-performance web server, ideal for static content
and reverse proxy services, efficient memory usage, load balancing, and
reverse proxy capabilities. And often used for serving static content or as a
reverse proxy for handling heavy traffic.
4. Database Management Systems (DBMS)
• MySQL: One of the most widely used relational databases, open-source with a
large community. And suitable for dynamic web applications that need to
manage structured data.
• PostgreSQL: An advanced open-source database known for its scalability,
performance, and extensibility. And ideal for complex data handling and
enterprise applications.
5. Domain Name System (DNS) Tools
• BIND: A widely used DNS server that manages domain name resolution and
critical for mapping domain names to IP addresses and handling DNS queries.
• Dnsmasq: Lightweight DNS forwarder and DHCP server and ideal for small to
medium-sized web server setups.
6. Security Tools
• UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall): A user-friendly firewall configuration tool for
managing firewall rules on Ubuntu and Debian-based servers. And essential
for restricting access to the server and securing web traffic.
• iptables: A powerful firewall tool that is part of the Linux kernel, used to filter
network traffic. And provides more advanced options for controlling incoming
and outgoing traffic.
• Fail2ban: A security tool that scans log files and bans IP addresses showing
signs of malicious activity (e.g., brute force attacks). And helps protect the
server from unauthorized access attempts.
7. Backup Tools
• Rsync: A powerful file synchronization and backup tool. And automates the
process of copying and synchronizing files and directories between servers
or local/remote locations.
• Duplicity: Backup software that supports encrypted and incremental
backups. And ideal for creating encrypted, secure backups of server data to
remote storage.

-- 24 of 132 --

16 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
8. Performance Monitoring Tools
• Nagios: A widely used open-source system and network monitoring tool.
And monitors server health, alerts you to performance issues, and ensures
uptime.
• Zabbix: A full-featured open-source monitoring tool for networks and
servers and provides detailed performance metrics and alerting for system
resources like CPU, memory, and disk usage.
• HTOP: An interactive system monitor tool for real-time tracking of server
performance and shows a dynamic overview of processes, memory usage,
and system load.
9. Configuration Management Tools
• Ansible: An open-source automation tool for configuration management,
deployment, and orchestration and automates the installation,
configuration, and management of server software, ensuring consistent
server environments.
• Puppet: A powerful configuration management tool for automating server
infrastructure and helps manage multiple servers and keep their
configurations consistent over time.
10. Web Hosting Control Panels
• cPanel: A paid, user-friendly control panel for managing web hosting, email,
databases, and security settings and simplifies the management of web
hosting environments, making it easier to control multiple websites and
domains.
• Webmin: A free, open-source control panel for Linux server administration
and offers a graphical interface for managing Linux systems, ideal for those
less comfortable with command-line operations.
11. Virtualization and Containerization Tools
• Docker: A containerization platform for deploying and managing
applications in isolated containers and helps run web applications in a
portable, scalable way, with minimal overhead.
• KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine): A full virtualization solution for Linux
on x86 hardware and allows you to create and manage virtual machines on
your Linux server, useful for hosting multiple isolated environments.

Key readings 2.1.1: Description of File system navigation
• ls (List Directory Contents): Lists the files and directories in the current working
directory.
✓ Common Options:
ls: Basic listing of files and directories.
ls -l: Lists files with detailed information (permissions, owner, size,
timestamp).
ls -a: Shows all files, including hidden files (those starting with.).
ls -la: Combines -l and -a to show detailed information for all files, including
hidden ones.
✓ Examples:
ls: Lists visible files and directories in the current directory.
ls -la /home/user: Shows detailed info for all files in the /home/user
directory, including hidden ones.
• l (Alias for ls -l): l is often an alias for ls -l in some Linux distributions or user-
defined configurations. It provides detailed information about files and
directories, such as permissions, ownership, size, and modification date.
• pwd (Print Working Directory): Displays the full path of the current working
directory.

Key readings 2.1.2: Description of basic commands for viewing current user
information
id: The id command displays the user ID (UID) and group ID (GID) of the current user,
along with supplementary group memberships.
1. getent: The getent command retrieves entries from system databases
configured in /etc/nsswitch.conf. It can be used to obtain information about
users, groups, and other system entities.
2. Whoami: The whoami command returns the username of the current user. It is
a simplified way to find out who is logged in.

Key readings 2.1.4: Description of Package management
• Installation
Installation involves adding new software packages to your system using a package
manager. Most package managers retrieve software from official repositories, which
are collections of software packages maintained and verified for the operating
system. The package manager ensures that all necessary dependencies (software
components required by the package) are installed alongside the desired package.
✓ Steps Involved:
The package manager resolves dependencies (other required software).
Downloads the package and dependencies from the repository.
Installs them on the system, setting up configuration files and system
services as needed.

• Ifconfig (Interface Configuration): is a command-line tool used in Unix-based systems

reachable.

troubleshooting.

Key readings 2.1.7: Description of task automation
1. at Command: The at command is used for one-time task scheduling. It allows
users to execute commands or scripts at a specific time in the future. Once the
task is executed, it will not repeat, unlike cron or anacron.
2. anacron Command: Anacron is designed for scheduling periodic tasks on
systems that are not guaranteed to be running all the time, such as laptops or
desktops that may be turned off. Unlike cron, anacron will run missed jobs once
the system is powered back on.
3. cron Command: Cron is one of the most widely used tools for scheduling
repetitive tasks. It allows users to schedule commands to run at specified
intervals such as minutes, hours, days, weeks, or months. Unlike anacron, cron
assumes the system will always be running, and missed jobs are not executed
later.

Description of file system navigation
● The ls command is used to list the contents of a directory.
● By default, it shows the names of files and directories in the current working
directory.
● It can be modified with options (like -l, -a, etc.) to provide additional details about
the files, such as file permissions, sizes, and hidden files.
● The command l is not a standard command in Linux by itself. However, it may be
an alias for ls -l in many systems.
● If defined as an alias, it would typically list files in the long format, displaying
detailed information such as permissions, owner, group, size, and last modification
date.
● The ls -la command provides a detailed list of all files and directories, including
hidden files (those beginning with a dot .).
● It displays information in a long format, including file permissions, number of links,
owner, group, size, and timestamp of the last modification.
● In contrast, ls alone only shows the names of non-hidden files and directories in a
simple list format.

● It displays the full path of the current directory in which the user is located.
● It helps users understand their location within the file system hierarchy.

● It is used to navigate between directories in the file system.

or to a different branch of the directory structure.
● Common usages include cd .. to move to the parent directory and cd ~ to return to
the home directory.

Key readings 2.2.1:Description of Linux files and directories
1. Directory Structure
✓ Root Directory (/): The top-level directory of the Linux file system hierarchy. All
other directories are subdirectories of /.
Example: /home, /etc, /var.
✓ Home Directory (/home): Contains personal directories for each user. For
example, /home/john would be the home directory for user john.
✓ Root User’s Home Directory (/root): The home directory for the root user
(superuser). It is separate from /home for security reasons.
✓ System Directories
/bin: Contains essential user binaries (commands) that are needed for basic
system operation and repair. Examples: ls, cp, mv.
/sbin: Contains system binaries used for system administration. These are
typically used by the root user. Examples: shutdown, ifconfig.
/etc: Contains system-wide configuration files and shell scripts. Examples:
/etc/passwd, /etc/fstab.

/var: Contains variable data like logs, mail spools, and temporary files that
are expected to grow in size. Examples: /var/log, /var/spool.
/tmp: Holds temporary files that are created by various programs. These
files are usually deleted upon reboot or after a certain period.
/dev: Contains device files that represent hardware components and
drivers. These are not regular files but rather interfaces to hardware.
Examples: /dev/sda (a disk), /dev/tty (a terminal).
/proc: A virtual file system that provides information about system
processes and hardware. Examples: /proc/cpuinfo (CPU information),
/proc/meminfo (memory usage).
/sys: A virtual file system that exposes kernel and device information.
o Usage: Provides a way to interact with the kernel and devices, often
used by system tools and utilities.
/usr: Contains user utilities and applications. It is the primary directory for
user software and libraries. Examples: /usr/bin, /usr/lib.
/opt: Used for installing third-party applications and software packages.
/mnt and /media: Used for mounting file systems, such as external drives
or network file systems.
2. File Permissions and Ownership
✓ File Permissions
Read (r): Allows viewing the contents of the file.
Write (w): Allows modifying the file.
Execute (x): Allows executing the file if it is a script or program.
✓ Permission Notation
Symbolic Notation: rwxr-xr,
Explanation: rwx (owner), r-x (group), r-- (others).
Octal Notation: 755
Explanation: 7 (owner: read, write, execute), 5 (group: read, execute), 5
(others: read, execute).
✓ Changing Permissions
chmod Command: Used to change file permissions.
Example: chmod 755 file.txt sets the permissions to rwxr-xr-x.
✓ Changing Ownership
chown Command: Used to change the owner and group of a file.
Example: chown user: group file.txt changes the owner to user and the
group to group.
3. Special Files and Links
✓ Symbolic Links: A symbolic link is a file that points to another file or directory.
Creation: ln -s target linkname

Example: ln -s /etc/hosts myhosts creates a symlink myhosts pointing to
/etc/hosts.
✓ Hard Links: A hard link is another name for an existing file on the file system. It
refers to the same inode.
Creation: ln target linkname
Example: ln file1 file2 creates a hard link file2 to file1.
4. Managing Files and Directories
✓ Creating and Deleting Directories

When creating a user, several attributes can be set:

2.2 User ID (UID)

the next available UID.
• To assign a specific UID: sudo useradd -u 1050 john
2.3 Primary Group

Description of user management
● Login Name is unique identifier assigned to each user in the Linux system, often
referred to as the username.
● Identification used for user authentication and to control access to resources.
● Format consists of alphanumeric characters, underscores, and cannot exceed a
certain length (usually 32 characters).
● File Storage for Login names are stored in the /etc/passwd file alongside user
information.
● Encrypted Password are stored in an encrypted format rather than as plain text to
enhance security.
● Uses cryptographic hash functions (e.g., SHA-512) to convert passwords into a
fixed-length string, making it difficult for attackers to retrieve the original
password.
● Encrypted passwords are usually stored in the /etc/shadow file, which is only
accessible by the root user.
● Protects user accounts from unauthorized access, ensuring that even if the
password file is compromised, the actual passwords remain secure.
● UID (User ID) is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each user in the system.
It helps the operating system track user permissions and ownership of files.
● GID (Group ID) is unique numerical identifier assigned to each user group. It
determines the access rights for all users within that group.
● Both UIDs and GIDs are used to enforce file permissions, control access to
resources, and facilitate multi-user environments.
● The root user typically has a UID of 0, while regular users start from UID 1000.
● The command-line interface that is loaded for a user when they log in. Common
shells include /bin/bash, /bin/sh, and /bin/zsh.

● The default shell determines the command syntax, available features (like scripting

users to customize their environment.

While creating a new user account in a Linux server choose a unique user ID and
descriptive username for easy identification.

● Assign a secure password for the new user. Ensure it complies with your
organization's password policies.
● Use passwd to set or change the user's password.
● Assign the user to a primary group, often a group with the same name as the user
or a specific group for development.
● Add the user to additional groups as needed (e.g., developers, admin).
● Ensure the user has the correct permissions for their files and directories.
● Manage group ownership and permissions for shared resources.

accessing the server.
Description of group management
● A group name is an identifier for a collection of users.
● It is used to manage permissions and access controls for files and resources.
● Group names can be used in commands to apply the same permissions or settings
to multiple users at once.

● GID (Group ID) is a unique numerical identifier assigned to each group in the
system.
● It is used by the operating system to manage group memberships and permissions.
● Each group has a corresponding GID that differentiates it from other groups.
● Group members are the users who belong to a specific group.
● You can list members of a group by examining the /etc/group file or using
commands like getent group <groupname>.
● Being a member of a group grants users the permissions associated with that group.
● A group password allows users to join a group if they know the password,
enhancing access control.
● This feature is rarely used in modern systems, as managing access through user and
group permissions is typically sufficient.
● Group passwords are set in the /etc/group file but may not be relevant for all
distributions.
● Group ownership refers to the association of a file or directory with a specific
group.
● The group ownership can affect the access permissions of the file for users
belonging to that group.
● You can change the group ownership of a file using the chgrp command.
● Group permissions determine what actions members of the group can perform on
a file or directory (read, write, execute).
● Permissions are set using the chmod command, and the group permissions can be
viewed using ls -l.
● Group permissions can help manage access to shared resources among users.
● A group expiration date can be set to limit the time a group can exist or to restrict

Key readings 2.4.1:Description of files and directories permissions
Types of Permissions:
• Read (r): Allows a file to be read or viewed.
• Write (w): Allows a file to be modified.
• Execute (x): Allows a file to be executed (run as a program/script) or a directory
to be accessed (e.g., changing into it with cd).
2. Permission Levels:
• User/Owner (u): The individual who owns the file or directory.
• Group (g): A set of users who share access to the file or directory.
• Others (o): All other users on the system who are not the owner or part of the
group.
3. Viewing Permissions:

78 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
• Use the ls -l command to view the permissions of files and directories. It shows
a string like rwxr-xr-- representing permissions for owner, group, and others
respectively.
4. Changing Permissions (chmod):
• Permissions can be altered using chmod either:
o Symbolically (e.g., chmod u+r to add read permission for the user).
o Numerically (e.g., chmod 755, where each digit represents the
permissions for user, group, and others in the form of a sum: r=4, w=2,
x=1).
5. Changing Ownership (chown):
• Ownership of a file or directory can be changed using the chown command. This
includes:
o Changing the user (e.g., chown user filename).
o Changing the group (e.g., chown user:group filename).
6. Special Permissions:
• Setuid (s): Applied to executables, allows users to execute the file with the
permissions of the file's owner.
• Setgid (s): Applied to files or directories, causes new files to inherit the group of
the directory.
• Sticky Bit (t): Used on directories to ensure only the file owner can delete or
modify files, even if other users have write permissions.
7. Directory Permissions:
• Read (r): Allows users to list the contents of a directory.
• Write (w): Allows users to create, delete, or rename files within the directory.
• Execute (x): Allows users to enter or access the directory, enabling cd to the
directory.
8. Recursive Permission Changes:
• To change permissions for all files and directories within a directory, use the -R
(recursive) option with chmod or chown.
9. Sticky Bit Use Case:
• Commonly applied to shared directories like /tmp. It ensures that users can only
delete or modify their own files within the directory.
10. Default Permissions (umask):
• The umask command sets the default permissions for newly created files and
directories. It subtracts permissions from the maximum possible (usually 666 for
files and 777 for directories).
11. Setting Group Permissions with g+s:
• Applying the setgid (g+s) on a directory ensures all files created in the directory
inherit the group of the directory rather than the user’s primary group.

Key readings 2.4.2: Applying files and directories permissions
1. Understanding Linux Permissions:
• File Permissions: Each file in Linux has three types of permissions:
o Read (r): Allows viewing the content of the file.
o Write (w): Allows modifying the content of the file.
o Execute (x): Allows running the file as a program (for executable files).
• Directory Permissions: For directories, the permissions have specific meanings:
o Read (r): Allows listing the contents of the directory.
o Write (w): Allows creating, deleting, or renaming files within the
directory.
o Execute (x): Allows accessing the directory (navigating into it).
2. Checking Current Permissions:
• Use the ls -l command to view the permissions of files and directories. The output
will look like this: drwxr-xr-- 2 user group 4096 Sep 29 10:00 mydirectory
-rw-r--r-- 1 user group 123 Sep 29 10:00 myfile.txt
• The first character indicates whether it's a directory (d) or a file (-). The next nine
characters are the permissions for user, group, and others.
3. Creating Users and Groups:

6. Setting Permissions with chmod:
• Symbolic Mode: Use chmod with letters to change permissions: sudo chmod
u+rwx,g+rx,o+r /path/to/directory # User gets read/write/execute, group gets
read/execute, others get read
• Numeric Mode: Use numbers to set permissions (where r=4, w=2, x=1):
sudo chmod 775 /path/to/directory # 7=4+2+1 for user, 7=4+2+1 for group, 5=4+1 for
others
7. Setting Special Permissions:
• Setgid (g+s): Ensures files created in a directory inherit the group of the
directory: sudo chmod g+s /path/to/directory
• Setuid (s): Allows users to execute a file with the permissions of the file’s owner:
sudo chmod u+s /path/to/executable
• Sticky Bit (t): Typically used on directories to allow only the owner to delete or
rename files: sudo chmod +t /path/to/directory
8. Verifying Permissions:
• After applying permissions, verify them using:
ls -ld /path/to/directory
ls -l /path/to/directory
9. Testing Access:
• Log in as different users or switch users using the su command to test whether
permissions are correctly applied: su - username
• Attempt to read, write, or execute files as different users to ensure permissions
are functioning as intended.
10. Monitoring and Auditing:
• Set up logging to monitor file access and changes, which can help in auditing and
security:
sudo apt install auditd

Description of files and directories permission
● The read permission allows a user to view the contents of a file or directory, a user
with read permission can open and read the file's contents, and a user with read
permission on a directory can list the files and subdirectories within it.
● The write permission allows a user to modify a file or directory, a user with write
permission can edit, delete, or create new content in the file, and a user with write
permission can add, remove, or rename files and subdirectories within the
directory.
● The execute permission allows a user to run a file as a program or script, a user
with execute permission can execute the file, provided it is a script or a binary
executable, and a user with execute permission on a directory can access the
directory's contents and perform actions on the files within it (but not necessarily
list them unless they also have read permission).
● Symbolic notation uses letters to represent permissions: r (read), w (write), and x
(execute) and permissions are typically represented in a string of 10 characters,
such as -rwxr-xr--.
● Octal notation is a numerical representation of file permissions, using numbers to
indicate permission levels, and each permission type corresponds to a specific value
Read = 4, Write = 2, and Execute = 1

4. To configure common DNS records within the DNS zone files
• Zone file location: Typically located in /var/named/ or /etc/bind/.
• A record: Maps a domain to an IP address.
• MX record: Defines mail server for the domain.
• PTR record: Used for reverse DNS lookup (in reverse zone file).
• SOA record: Defines the Start of Authority, which should be properly
configured for each zone.
5. Testing tools:
• Use dig to query specific DNS records: dig example.com A or dig -x
192.168.1.10 for reverse lookup.
• Use nslookup to test domain resolution: nslookup example.com.
• Check DNS service status: Run systemctl status named (or bind9) to check if
the DNS service is active.
• Log file checks: Look into DNS logs (/var/log/messages or /var/log/syslog) for
any error messages or query logs.
• Syntax checks: Use named-checkconf for configuration file syntax and named-
checkzone to validate zone file correctness.

Key readings 3.2.1.: Description of DHCP services
1. Description of DHCP Handshake Operations
• DHCP Discovery: Client broadcasts a request to find a DHCP server.
• DHCP Offer: DHCP server responds with an IP address offer and network
settings (subnet mask, gateway, DNS, etc.).
• DHCP Request: Client selects an offer and sends a request to the server,
asking to use the provided IP.
• DHCP Acknowledgment: DHCP server confirms the IP assignment and sends
a final acknowledgment, completing the handshake.
2. Install DHCP Server Package
• Linux Systems: Use isc-dhcp-server for Linux-based systems like Ubuntu.
o Install with: sudo apt-get install isc-dhcp-server
• Windows Systems: The DHCP server role is installed via the Server Manager
or PowerShell.
• Ensure the server has a static IP: Dynamic IP on the DHCP server itself may
cause issues during network configuration.
3. DHCP Configuration Files
• Location:
✓ Linux: /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf is the primary configuration file.
✓ Windows: Managed through the DHCP Manager GUI or PowerShell.

4. Set the DHCP Server Parameters
• IP Range: Set the range of IP addresses to be assigned to clients.
o Example: range 192.168.1.100 192.168.1.200;
• Lease Time: Define default and maximum lease times to control how long IP
addresses are assigned.
o Example: default-lease-time 600; max-lease-time 7200;
• Network Details: Include the subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS server
options.
o Example: option routers 192.168.1.1; option domain-name-servers
192.168.1.20;
• Domain Name: Set the domain name to be assigned to clients.
o Example: option domain-name "mv_tvet.ac.rw";
• Static IP Reservations: Reserve specific IPs for important devices (servers,
printers) by mapping MAC addresses to IP addresses.

Key readings 3.2.2: Configuring DHCP services
1. Description of DHCP Handshake Operations: The DHCP handshake involves a
sequence of messages between a DHCP client and server:
• Discovery: The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER message to find available
DHCP servers.
• Offer: The server responds with a DHCPOFFER message, offering an IP
address and other network configurations.
• Request: The client responds with a DHCPREQUEST message, requesting the
offered IP address.
• Acknowledgment: The server sends a DHCPACK message, confirming the IP
address allocation and providing the client with network settings.
• Install DHCP Server Package: On a Linux system, you can typically install the
DHCP server package using a package manager.
2. DHCP Configuration Files: The main configuration file for the DHCP server is
usually located at /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf. This file contains settings for network
pools, leases, and options.
3. Set the DHCP Server Parameters: Configure the DHCP server by editing the
configuration file (/etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf). You need to set parameters such as:
• Subnet: Define the subnet and IP address range.
• Range: Specify the range of IP addresses to be assigned to clients.
• Options: Set options like default gateway, DNS servers, and lease time.
Description of DHCP services
● The DHCP handshake process involves four steps: Discover, Offer, Request, and

● To install a DHCP server on Linux, use package managers like apt for Debian-based

# Indicative content 3.3: Configuration of File Server Service

Indicative content 3.3: Configuration of File Server Service
1: Answer the following questions:
i. What is SMB/CIFS, and how is it typically used in network environments?
ii. Explain the role of NFS in file sharing on Unix/Linux networks?
iii. What is FTP, and how does it differ from other file sharing protocols like SMB and
NFS?
2: Present the findings to trainer, your colleagues or to the whole class
3: Address any questions or concerns
4. Read key reading 3.3.1 in their manuals.
Key readings 3.3.1: Description of file Server service
1. Definition of SMB/CIFS
SMB/CIFS is a network file sharing protocol primarily used for sharing files,
printers, and serial ports between systems, especially in Windows
environments.
2. Key Features:
• Cross-Platform Support: Although originally designed for Windows, SMB is
now supported on multiple platforms, including Linux and macOS.
• Authentication: Supports user authentication to control access to shared
resources.
• File and Record Locking: Prevents multiple users from editing the same file
simultaneously, ensuring data integrity.
• Versioning: SMB has several versions, such as SMBv1, SMBv2, and SMBv3,
with newer versions offering better security and performance.
• Encryption: SMBv3 introduces encryption to protect data in transit,
reducing the risk of eavesdropping.
• Windows Integration: Tight integration with Active Directory (AD) for
managing user permissions and access controls.
3. Considerations:
• Ensure that SMBv1 is disabled as it has known security vulnerabilities.
• SMB is chattier (higher network overhead) compared to other protocols.
Duration: 7 hrs

• Firewall settings should be configured to allow SMB ports (445 for direct
SMB and 139 for NetBIOS over TCP).
4. NFS (Network File System): NFS is a file-sharing protocol widely used in
UNIX/Linux environments to share directories and files across a network.
5. Key Features:
• Stateless Protocol: NFS is designed to be stateless, meaning the server
doesn’t maintain session information for clients. This makes it easier to
recover from client or server failures.
• File Locking: NFS provides optional support for file locking, ensuring that
concurrent file access doesn’t lead to data corruption.
• Permissions and Access Control: NFS relies on the Unix permissions system
(UIDs and GIDs) to manage access control.
• Versions: NFS has several versions (NFSv3, NFSv4), with NFSv4 offering
improvements in security (support for Kerberos authentication) and
performance.
• Integration with Linux: It is highly integrated into Linux and UNIX operating
systems and works well in environments where centralized file storage is
needed.
6. Considerations:
• Firewall Configuration: Ensure that the required NFS ports (111, 2049) are
open.
• Security: Use NFSv4 for better security (Kerberos-based authentication)
and encrypted file transfers.
• UID/GID Mapping: Ensure proper user ID mapping between clients and
servers to avoid permission issues.
• NFS might not perform well in environments where there is high network
latency due to its stateless nature.
7. FTP (File Transfer Protocol): FTP is a standard protocol used for transferring files
between a client and server over a TCP-based network, such as the internet.
8. Key Features:
• Basic Authentication: FTP uses simple username and password
authentication, though these credentials are transmitted in plaintext.
• Active vs. Passive Mode: FTP supports two communication modes—active
and passive. In active mode, the client opens a port for data transfer, while
in passive mode, the server opens the port.
• Anonymous FTP: Allows users to download public files from servers
without providing login credentials.
• File Transfer: FTP is ideal for large file transfers and supports both binary
and ASCII modes for file transmission.

-- 112 of 132 --

104 | L i n u x S e r v e r A d m i n i s t r a t i o n – T r a i n e e M a n u a l
• Directory Navigation: FTP allows users to navigate the server’s directory
structure and upload/download files.
9. Considerations:
• Security: FTP is inherently insecure as it transmits data, including
passwords, in plaintext. For secure file transfers, consider using SFTP
(Secure FTP) or FTPS (FTP over SSL).
• Firewall Configuration: Ensure appropriate ports (21 for command, 20
for data) are open, and configure firewalls accordingly for passive/active
modes.
• Encryption: Use FTPS or SFTP to encrypt data in transit for sensitive
information.
10. FTP has high latency sensitivity, meaning network delays can negatively affect
performance, especially in high-latency environments.

Points to Remember
Description of file Server service
● SMB (Server Message Block) is a protocol for sharing files, printers, and other
resources, primarily in Windows environments but supported across platforms like
Linux through Samba. CIFS is a dialect of SMB used for file sharing over the internet.
● SMB/CIFS provides features like user authentication, access control, and remote
file access. It operates over TCP/IP (port 445) and supports both TCP and UDP
communication.

● NFS (Network File System) is a distributed file system primarily used in Unix/Linux
environments for file sharing. It is stateless, uses port 2049, and is suitable for data
centers and environments requiring centralized data access.
● FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is focused on file transfers, ideal for
uploading/downloading files between hosts. It operates over port 21 for
commands and uses additional ports for data transfer.
● Differences: SMB/CIFS and NFS focus on file sharing and resource management,
whereas FTP is designed for file transfers. SMB/CIFS is common in Windows, NFS in
Linux/Unix, and FTP is platform-independent but widely used in web hosting.

● Install Samba (the open-source implementation of SMB/CIFS) using the package
manager (apt install samba for Ubuntu/Debian or yum install samba for
CentOS/RHEL).
● For Windows: SMB is built into Windows and can be enabled/disabled via "Turn
Windows Features On or Off."
● Edit the smb.conf file in /etc/samba/ to define shared directories, access controls,
and authentication settings.
● Ensure the Samba service is enabled to start automatically after a system reboot.
● Open the necessary firewall ports (TCP 445 for SMB, TCP 139 for NetBIOS over TCP).
● Test the configuration by connecting to the server using another machine with the
SMB/CIFS protocol.
● Install the NFS server package (apt install nfs-kernel-server on Ubuntu/Debian or
yum install nfs-utils on CentOS/RHEL).
● Define shared directories in the /etc/exports file. Specify which clients are allowed
access and their permission levels (e.g., read-only or read-write).
● Open the necessary firewall ports (TCP/UDP 2049 for NFS).
● Test the NFS server by mounting the shared directories on a client machine and
verifying file access
● Install an FTP server package (e.g., vsftpd or proftpd) using the package manager
(apt install vsftpd or yum install vsftpd).
● Edit the FTP configuration file (e.g., /etc/vsftpd.conf) to set parameters like
anonymous access, local user permissions, and file directories.
● Ensure that the FTP service starts automatically after system boot and is running
properly.
● Open FTP ports (21 for command, 20 for data). Configure firewall rules for active or
passive FTP mode, depending on the use case.

● Use FTPS (FTP over SSL) for encrypted file transfers to enhance security.
● Test the FTP server by connecting to it from a client using an FTP client or web
browser and transferring files.
● Define the root directory for FTP users, where they will land upon connection. In
vsftpd.conf, this is typically set using the local_root directive.
● Disable anonymous access (anonymous_enable=NO) for better security.
● Set up user authentication by allowing local users (local_enable=YES), ensuring that
only authenticated users can access the FTP server.
● For networks with firewalls, Passive Mode might be preferable to avoid firewall
issues. Configure passive mode settings in the configuration file.
● Define share permissions in the smb.conf file for shared folders. Control access by
specifying users or groups that are allowed to read/write.
● Use Linux’s file permissions (chmod and chown) to manage access at the filesystem
level.
● Samba’s built-in authentication can be used to control access for specific users or
groups, using smbpasswd to manage passwords.
● Set permissions in the /etc/exports file to define which clients can access the NFS
shares and whether they have read-only or read-write access.
● Use Unix/Linux permissions (chmod, chown) to control file-level access once NFS
clients are connected.
● Use root squash (an option in /etc/exports) to prevent root users on client
machines from having root privileges on the NFS server.
● Set user access controls in the FTP server configuration (vsftpd.conf). Control
whether anonymous users or local users can access the server.
● Use local user directories and set read/write permissions to control what users can
do with files.
● Use chroot jail to limit users’ file access to their home directories
(chroot_local_user=YES).
● Regularly back up shared files using tools like rsync, tar, or backup software such as
Bacula or Amanda.
● Create a cron job to automate the backup of critical directories.
● Ensure backup files are stored both locally and on remote locations (e.g., cloud
storage or offsite servers).
● Test recovery by restoring files from backups periodically to ensure that the
backups are functional.

Key readings 3.4.1.: Description of web server
1. Definition of a Web Server
A web server is software or hardware that stores, processes, and delivers web pages
to clients (browsers) over the internet using HTTP/HTTPS protocols. It serves static
or dynamic content (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, etc.) requested by users.
2. Types of Web Servers for Linux:
• Apache HTTP Server: The most popular open-source web server known for
its flexibility and wide use. It supports dynamic content via modules.
• Nginx: A lightweight, high-performance web server with a strong focus on
concurrency and low resource usage. It excels at handling large numbers of
simultaneous connections.
• Other Servers: Lighttpd, Caddy, and OpenLiteSpeed also offer web serving
capabilities for specific use cases.
3. Configuration Files: The configuration files for web servers define settings such
as ports, document roots, server names, and security rules.
• Apache: /etc/apache2/apache2.conf or /etc/httpd/httpd.conf
• Nginx: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf or /etc/nginx/sites-available/default

4. Installation of Apache HTTP Server:
• Use the package manager to install:
• Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install apache2
• CentOS/RHEL: sudo yum install httpd
• Start the service and enable it on boot: sudo systemctl start apache2 (or
httpd for CentOS).
5. Installation of Nginx:
• Similarly, install Nginx via the package manager:
• Ubuntu/Debian: sudo apt install nginx
• CentOS/RHEL: sudo yum install nginx
• Start and enable it on boot: sudo systemctl start nginx.
6. Firewall Configuration:
• Open ports for HTTP (80) and HTTPS (443) to allow web traffic:
• UFW (Ubuntu): sudo ufw allow 'Apache Full' or sudo ufw allow 'Nginx Full'
• FirewallD (CentOS): sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent and
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent.
7. Verify the Installation:
• Use a browser to visit http://your_server_ip and ensure the default page is
displayed.
• Verify the web server status:
• Apache: sudo systemctl status apache2
• Nginx: sudo systemctl status nginx
8. Permissions:
• Ensure proper permissions are set for the web server’s root directory
(/var/www/html) to prevent unauthorized access:
• Ownership: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
• Permissions: sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html
• Only allow the web server user (e.g., www-data) write access to sensitive
files.
9. Encryption:
• Protect web server communication by using SSL/TLS encryption to secure
data transferred between the server and clients.
• Use strong ciphers and SSL/TLS protocols to minimize security
vulnerabilities.

sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=http --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --add-
service=https --permanent.
● Use a browser to visit http://your_server_ip and ensure the default page is
displayed.
● Ensure proper permissions are set for the web server’s root directory
(/var/www/html) to prevent unauthorized access
● Protect web server communication by using SSL/TLS encryption to secure data
transferred between the server and clients.
● Use strong ciphers and SSL/TLS protocols to minimize security vulnerabilities.
● SSL Certificates are essential for securing HTTPS connections. Use self-signed
certificates for internal testing or Let’s Encrypt for free public certificates.
● Configure the web server to use SSL by enabling the SSL module and specifying the
certificate paths in the configuration file.
● Verify the SSL certificate by accessing the web server via https://your_server_ip.

encryption, and SSL certificates. As a network administrator, you are required to install

# Indicative content 3.5: Configuration of Mail Server Service

Indicative content 3.5: Configuration of Mail Server Service
1: Answer the following questions:
i. What are the key components of an email server, and what roles do they play
in the email delivery process?
ii. What log files are important for monitoring the email server, and what key
metrics should you track for performance and troubleshooting?
iii. What methods can you use to test the functionality of the email server, and
how can you optimize its performance for better efficiency?
iv. What strategies should be employed to ensure regular backups of the email server,
and what steps are necessary to recover from a disaster?
2: Present your findings to the trainer or the whole class
3: Address any questions or concerns.
5: Read the Key readings 3.5.1 in their manuals
Key readings 3.5.1: Description of Mail server services
• SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol): Protocol used for sending emails from
client to server and between servers.
• IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol): Allows users to access and manage
their emails directly on the server, supporting multiple device synchronization.
• POP3 (Post Office Protocol): Downloads emails from the server to the local
client, often removing them from the server.
• Mail Transfer Agent (MTA): Software responsible for routing and delivering
email (e.g., Postfix).
• Mail Delivery Agent (MDA): Delivers email to user mailboxes (e.g., Dovecot).
• Mail User Agent (MUA): Client software used by users to send and receive
emails (e.g., Outlook, Thunderbird).
• Set Up of SMTP Server (Postfix)
✓ Installation: Use package manager commands (apt or yum) to install Postfix.
✓ Configuration: Set essential parameters in /etc/postfix/main.cf, including

Key readings 3.5.2:Configuring mail server services
1. Choose the Right Mail Server Software
• Postfix, Send mail, and Exim are popular SMTP server options.
• For incoming mail, consider Dovecot or Courier for IMAP/POP3 services.
Practical Activity 3.5.2: Configuring mail server services
Task:
